newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ's accommodative stance may backfire - experts.
newsitem.headline: BOJ's accommodative stance may backfire - experts.

text.p: The Bank of Japan's accommodative operations in the money market, intended to aid banks and the stock market by easing upward pressure on short-term lending rates, could instead fuel such pressure, market experts say.

In its zeal to hold the key overnight call rate below 0.50 percent, they said, the BOJ was encouraging banks to borrow short-term instead of long-term funds, igniting a vicious circle that will force the central bank to keep pumping money into the market.

"City banks will probably think they may as well borrow funds through the overnight call market if sufficient liquidity is going to be supplied (by the BOJ)," said Shin Nagai, treasurer at ABN AMRO Bank NV's Tokyo branch.
The BOJ conducted an accommodative money market operation last Friday for the first time since August 7 last year, and continued its accommodative stance on Monday and Tuesday.

The move, sparked by last week's rise in the key overnight call rate to 0.55 percent, was seen by analysts as an effort to help shore up banks' profitability, buoy the stock market and ease worries about the health of Japan's financial system.
But it will also stoke borrowers' appetite for short-term funds and this will add to upward pressure on rates, Nagai said.
The overnight call rate had already been rising in response to demand for funds ahead of the fiscal year-end on March 31.

Nagai said borrowers such as city banks were reassured by the BOJ's statement last Friday that it will adhere to a commitment it made in September 1995 to keep call rates below 0.50 percent on average.

As a result, borrowers will see little risk of interest rates rising soon and are likely to continue borrowing funds through the overnight call market, which offers lower interest rates than long-term funds do, he added.
On Monday, the key overnight call rate's weighted average was 0.48 percent, while one-month certificates of deposit were traded at 0.55 percent.
The central bank decided to inject extra liquidity into the money market to prevent worries about the financial system from flaring up again, said Totan Research Co president Shoji Kitta.

"If the BOJ had allowed interest rates to rise it may have led to a situation in which worries over the financial system were re-ignited towards the end of March. Its decision to conduct accommodative operations was aimed at preventing this," Kitta said.
Low short-term interest rates help banks hold down funding costs and increase their profits, Kitta said.
Worries about weak stock prices may also be responsible for the BOJ's accommodative operations, said Yasunari Ueno, chief market economist at Fuji Securities.

"Until the end of the current fiscal year government officials are likely to make a lot of comments (to boost the stock market). The BOJ's accommodative operation could be part of that effort," Ueno said.
The benchmark overnight call rate stood at around 0.49 percent after the BOJ's operation on Tuesday, up from Monday's weighted average of 0.48 percent.

The key stock market barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, gained 135.65 points on Tuesday to close at 18,564.78. But it was still down nearly 800 points from where it stood at the end of 1996. --Tokyo Treasury Desk, +81-3-5473-3748
